hints: Sketch the two S-shaped curves in your head. At any same partial pressure of oxygen in the middle of the graph, is the right-shifted curve higher or lower in % saturation than the left-shifted curve?
Remember the golden rule: shift right means lower affinity and easier unloading, shift left means higher affinity and harder unloading. Which option describes easier unloading in respiring tissues?
walkthrough:
**Read the axes of the dissociation curve**

Think of the graph simply. The x-axis is partial pressure of oxygen ($pO_2$) and the y-axis is % saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen.

A curve to the right means that at any given $pO_2$, saturation is lower than for a curve to the left.

**Translate right shift into affinity**

Lower saturation at the same $pO_2$ means the haemoglobin is holding onto oxygen less tightly.

In biology language:
$$\text{right shift = lower affinity = gives up } O_2 \text{ more easily}$$

**Apply it to small mammals**

Smaller mammals have a larger surface area to volume ratio and a higher metabolic rate, so they need to release oxygen to respiring tissues quickly.

A right-shifted curve is perfect for this, as it unloads oxygen more easily at tissue $pO_2$. That points straight to C.

options.A: False. At low $pO_2$ a right-shifted curve has lower saturation, so it binds oxygen less strongly, not more strongly.
options.B: False. A right-shifted curve needs a higher $pO_2$ to reach full saturation, not a lower one. Left shift would saturate earlier.
options.C: Correct. Right shift means lower affinity, so haemoglobin unloads and releases oxygen to tissues more easily, which suits the high metabolic demand of small mammals.
options.D: False. At high $pO_2$ both curves flatten near 100% saturation, so both carry about the same maximum amount of oxygen.
